source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in Chess
url: local PDF copy of Cognitive Psychology 4, 55-61
finding: Original result. With real game positions, recall after 5 s tracked playing strength. With random positions there was no relation at all between memory and strength.
numbers: N = 3 (master M, class A player A, beginner B). New puzzle-book positions, one 5 s trial: B 33%, A 49%, M 81% correct, versus 18%, 34%, 62% on the first trial of the earlier positions. On random positions all three did worse than B on game positions.
quote: In the random, unstructured positions there was no relation at all between memory of the position and playing strength.
limits: Three subjects only; the master was out of practice and in his forties. Positions were not all quiet. De Groot noted that guessing the average master position gives about 44% correct, so a high score is not all memory.
agent_relevance: The founding claim is that skill lives in stored patterns, not in raw capacity. It is also a three-person result that later work softened (see b05, b19). Do not build on 'no skill effect on random input' as a law.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions: implications for the theory of expertise
finding: Mirror-image reflection of real positions hurt recall more as skill rose, and the size of the drop matched a simulation in which every chunk is tied to a specific place and colour.
numbers: Experiment 2, N = 25 (5 Masters, 11 Experts, 9 Class A). Normal plus horizontal-flip positions: 77.3%, 49.7%, 34.5% correct (Masters, Experts, Class A). Vertical plus central flip: 62.9%, 38.6%, 27.5%. Mean drop 10.3% in humans versus 11.4% in simulation. Skill x modification interaction F(2,22) = 3.48, p < .05. Vertical-axis contrast F(1,22) = 96.79, p < .001.
quote: chess information, or at least much of its pattern-recognizing component, encodes both the color and the precise location of the pieces.
limits: Drop is small (about 10 points) and recall stayed far above random-position level. Chunk-size effects were non-significant (p = .07). Players did not notice the flips. A later study (b21) argues for more abstract role-based encoding.
agent_relevance: Pattern cues in experts are fairly literal and position-bound. An agent memory keyed on exact surface form will miss a mirrored or relabelled twin of a stored problem; a core-plus-slots key should tolerate relabelling. Test retrieval on flipped and renamed variants.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions
finding: Same N = 25 study, random-position control. Game positions beat random positions by a very large margin. Skill differences in chunk size appeared only for game positions, not for random ones. The skill gain on random recall was positive but not significant.
numbers: Game vs random F(1,22) = 291.51, p < .001. Skill x type F(2,22) = 16.50, p < .001. Skill effect on random recall F(2,22) = 0.18, ns. Largest chunk, game positions: 11.2, 7.4, 6.2 pieces (Masters, Experts, Class A); random: 4.1, 4.3, 4.1. Chunks per position, game: 4.0, 4.3, 2.5; random: 1.2, 1.7, 1.8.
quote: The substantial superiority in recall of high-rated over low-rated players that appears regularly when normal game positions are used as stimuli nearly disappears
limits: Only 3 to 5 random positions per subject. Chunk counts use a 2 s inter-piece cut-off and include wrong pieces. Low power for the random-position skill test.
agent_relevance: A clean control: an expert-pattern advantage should shrink when structure is destroyed. For an agent, run template-memory ablations on scrambled problems; a gain that survives scrambling is not from pattern recall.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions
finding: Rival account tested: Holding's idea that chunks are abstract and independent of colour and location. The mirror data and simulation rejected the extreme version, so the estimate of about 50,000 chunks for a Master was not shown to be too high.
numbers: Chunks per position 3.8 (Masters), 4.1 (Experts), 2.3 (Class A); largest chunk per position 10.1, 7.1, 6.1 pieces (skill F(2,22) = 4.70, p < .05). Errors of commission follow an inverted U with skill (Experts most; F(2,22) = 7.65, p < .005). Template cores described as about a dozen pieces; learning one may take hours.
quote: we must reject his conclusion that the number of chunks in an expert's memory is much smaller than the 50,000 estimated by Chase and Simon.
limits: The 50,000 figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a measurement. Template core size and learning time are stated by the authors as expectations, not measured here.
agent_relevance: Competing view (few abstract schemas) versus many literal chunks. Practical read: expect a large store of specific, small patterns to matter, plus a smaller set of slotted templates for frequent situations.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories (Cognition 66, 115-152)
url: local PDF copy of the preprint
finding: Review of about a dozen experiments on random positions shown 10 s or less. Skill correlates with recall even there, but rarely reaches significance, because samples and effects are small. This corrects the textbook claim of zero skill effect.
numbers: At 5 s on random positions Masters place on average 5.5 pieces, the weakest players (below class B) 2.6 pieces. Chase and Simon 1973 found no difference with 3 subjects.
quote: strong players do maintain some superiority when recalling briefly presented random positions.
limits: Author is a template-theory proponent reviewing his own earlier synthesis. Numbers are as reported in the review, not re-derived from the original studies.
agent_relevance: Lesson for evidence handling: a famous null (random positions) was an underpowered small-N result. Treat 'no effect' claims from tiny samples as unsettled.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories
url: local PDF copy of the preprint
finding: Interference studies were the main empirical problem for the original chunking theory. If chunks live only in short-term memory, a distracting task should wipe the position out. It did not.
numbers: Charness 1976: 30 s delay with rehearsal or interfering task, recall fell only 6 to 8%. Even chess-material interference (finding the best move, naming pieces on another board) gave no significant loss. Frey & Adesman 1976: two boards of 8 s each, then 3 s or 30 s of counting backward, only a small loss versus one board. Multi-board recall extended to 5 boards (Gobet & Simon 1996) and 9 boards (Cooke et al. 1993, 8 s each); limit for about 60% accuracy is around four or five boards.
limits: 1970s to 1990s studies with small samples. The reviewer calls them discriminating but not decisive, since SEEK and long-term working memory can also explain them.
agent_relevance: Information must reach long-term storage fast. For an agent this argues for writing a pattern into memory at first sight (slot filling), not after repeated exposure.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories
url: local PDF copy of the preprint
finding: Four theories compared on chess recall: chunking (Chase & Simon 1973), SEEK (Holding 1985), long-term working memory (Ericsson & Kintsch 1995) and template theory. The areas that separate them best are random and distorted positions, very short presentation, and interference. Chunking fits more data than its critics claim, but template theory fits best.
numbers: No single effect size. The ranking by fit to the empirical areas is the author's own judgement.
quote: Contrary to recurrent criticisms in the literature, it is shown that the chunking theory is consistent with most of the data.
limits: Template theory's author did the ranking. No independent referee comparison. Long-term working memory theory was judged too vague to give quantitative predictions (also stated in Gobet & Clarkson 2004).
agent_relevance: Which rival wins matters less than which experiment splits them. For agent memory designs, copy the habit: pick tests (scrambled input, short exposure, interruption) where two designs predict different outcomes.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards (Cognitive Psychology 31, 1-40)
finding: Experiment 2: recall of several boards shown in sequence rose with the pause between boards, which the original chunking theory (STM only) cannot explain. Masters gained more than Experts.
numbers: One board: Masters 92.3%, Experts 64.5% (game); random: 21.1% and 17.7%. Four boards (100 pieces) with 10 s pause: Masters replaced 82.9 pieces, Experts 44.9. Gain from 1 s to 10 s pause: Masters +71% (two boards) and +63% (four boards); Experts +40% and +33%. No serial-position effect pooled (48 to 51% per board).
limits: Few Masters; a Grandmaster missing one board pulled an average down. Small cells. Measures recall of pieces, not move choice.
agent_relevance: Time to link new material to existing structure matters. An agent that gets a moment to file a new case against its stored templates should keep more than one that must hold it in context alone.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory
finding: Boundary condition: with many boards, the percentage recalled falls to about what guessing from the typical master position would give, so the apparent huge capacity needs care.
numbers: Experiment 1: three Masters fell from about 95% (one board) to 39% (five boards). Cooke et al. 1993: two Masters from about 90% to about 50% (five) and about 40% (nine boards), read from a graph. De Groot's average-position guessing baseline: 43.7%. Cooke's best subject still beat the baseline on seven of nine boards (11 pieces on average).
limits: Percentages near the guessing floor mean the claim of nine boards held rests on a few well-above-chance subjects. Authors use the baseline to bound the claim, not to refute it. Cooke figures are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Always compute the prior-only baseline. Part of 'memory' is a default template with typical values; an agent test needs the same floor (answer from the generic template alone).

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory, Experiment 3
finding: Training case: one Chessmaster raised, over many sessions, the number of boards he could reproduce above 70% average accuracy to nine, placing up to 160 pieces correctly in a session.
numbers: N = 1 subject. Peak of nine boards at block 18, then about eight positions. Session 90: 10 positions attempted, 160 pieces correct.
limits: Single subject, possible retrieval-structure strategy beyond templates, no control group. Shows what is possible, not what is typical.
agent_relevance: Memory skill is trainable with deliberate practice on the task, but one case proves little. Do not generalise to training gains for a scaffold without measuring.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory (Cognitive Science 24, 651-682)
finding: Human data from 1 to 60 s. Masters recognise a lot in the first second and saturate after about 3 s; weaker players keep improving. This fits fast recognition of templates plus slower learning of new chunks. A CHREST simulation fits closely but under-predicts Masters.
numbers: N = 20 (5 Masters, 8 Experts, 7 Class A), ratings 1770 to 2595. Masters at 1 s match Experts at 10 s. Skill groups differ at 10 s or less: F(2,16) = 27.63, p < .001. Experts' largest chunk grows from 9 to 10 pieces to about 17 at 60 s; Class A from 4 to 5 pieces. Simulation under-estimated Masters at 5 s by about 8%.
limits: Masters were not given game positions over 10 s (ceiling), so their curve is cut. One extra subject quit. Model fit is good but imperfect for Masters; the 300K-node net size is a guess.
agent_relevance: Two components: instant recognition (templates) and slower learning. A scaffold could separate 'cheap lookup first' from 'build a new pattern after' and measure each.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty?
finding: Random positions also show a skill effect at every exposure time, but a smaller one than game positions. Skill raised both the amount encoded in the first second and the rate of later gain.
numbers: Random positions: skill groups differ at 10 s or less F(2,15) = 7.74, p < .005, and above 10 s F(2,16) = 14.36, p < .001. Logistic fit: learning rate c doubles from Class A to Experts and triples to Masters; first-second amount (100-B) rises 1.5 and 2 times. Both parameters are much larger for game than for random positions.
limits: Only one random position per duration per subject (10 in all). Wide spread inside groups.
agent_relevance: Even novel material gives experts a small edge: chance matches with a large pattern store. A big pattern library helps a little on unfamiliar problems, at a rate worth measuring rather than assuming zero or large.

source: Gobet & Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory: evidence for the magical number four ... or is it two? (Memory 12, 732-747)
finding: Direct test of chunking (about 7 chunks, small chunks) against template theory (about 3 chunks, large chunks). The same 12 players did recall and copy tasks on a physical board and on a computer. In the computer condition fewer than three chunks were replaced and Masters used very large chunks.
numbers: N = 12 (4 Masters, 4 Class B, 4 novices; mean age 22.5). Recall of game positions 70.0%, 45.0%, 17.0%; random 22.3%, 16.9%, 14.4%. Skill x position F(2,9) = 12.14, p < .01. Skill effect on random positions not significant. Display effect on chunk size F(1,9) = 76.16, p < .001.
quote: the original chunking theory overestimated short-term memory capacity and underestimated the size of chunks used
limits: Only 4 per skill group, so the random-position skill test has little power. A chunk is defined by a 2 s pause, an operational proxy. Participants aged 15 to 35.
agent_relevance: The 'seven chunks' number is not stable; it depends on how chunks are measured. Do not hard-code a working-memory size from chess into a scaffold.

source: Gobet & Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory
finding: Chunk size depends on the presentation medium, a hand-size artifact that explains the gap between Chase & Simon (1973) and Gobet & Simon (1998). Masters' maximum chunk was about twice as large on screen as with physical pieces.
numbers: Masters, game positions, median largest chunk: recall 14.8 pieces on screen vs 7.5 on board; copy 12.9 vs 3.8. Class B recall 9.0, novices 6.3 (screen). Random positions, Masters on screen: 6.7 (recall), 7.9 (copy); on board 3.3 and 3.1 for all groups. Chase & Simon master median largest chunk: 5 pieces.
limits: Chunk defined by 2 s timing. Copy-task chunks can be inflated by learning during viewing: with views over 3 s, chunk size correlates with viewing time (r = .71 Masters, .52 Class B, .63 novices, all p < .01), but not with views under 3 s (slightly negative).
agent_relevance: A measured unit depends on the instrument. When we measure 'template size' in an agent, keep the measuring method fixed and check it is not just the time or context length given.

source: Gobet & Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory
finding: Large chunks exist even under very short viewing, and the share of large chunks rises with skill, as the template account predicts. The number of chunks in the recall task stays small. Singly placed pieces are mostly guesses.
numbers: Copy task on screen with view under 3 s: 67% (Masters), 41% (Class B), 12% (novices) of chunks had 4 or more pieces. One Class B player had an 11-piece chunk in 1.83 s. Recall on screen: fewer than 3 chunks always; random positions 1.5 to 1.9 chunks. In random positions on screen, 21 of 194 pieces were placed singly and only 6 of those 21 were correct (28.6%).
limits: Few observations under 2 s; the 3 s threshold and the size of 4 were post hoc definitions. Singly placed pieces were excluded from the chunk count as guesses, a choice that shapes the count.
agent_relevance: Singleton retrievals are mostly noise: a retrieval that returns one weak fragment is often a wrong guess. Require a multi-element match before a retrieved pattern is used as a cue.

source: Waters & Gobet (2008) Mental imagery and chunks: empirical and computational findings (Memory & Cognition)
finding: Out-of-sample test of CHREST: pieces placed on intersections of squares (not centres) cut recall, and net size mattered more for game positions than for randomised ones, as the model predicted. The fit supports a serial 125 ms per piece shift in the mind's eye.
numbers: N = 36 players (weak amateurs to grandmasters). CHREST nets of 1k to 300k nodes. Intersection positions: 300k net 44.8% vs 1k net 23.7% on game positions; on fully randomised positions 10.7% vs 4.1%. Net-size effect per position type: game 0.173, 1/3 0.092, 2/3 0.050, random 0.051, fully random 0.057. Net size x position type F(4,8) = 66.1, p < .001.
limits: The model has free parameters elsewhere (timing, net size), held from the earlier fit. The bishop-versus-knight result is a post hoc Stroop-style explanation.
agent_relevance: A good model gives a quantitative prediction that fails when its main assumption is removed. Write such a prediction for any template memory we add (what falls, by how much, when pattern structure is scrambled).

source: Gobet & Waters (2003) The role of constraints in expert memory (JEP: LMC)
finding: Discriminating experiment between template theory and the rival constraint-attunement hypothesis (Vicente & Wang 1998). On truly random positions (location and piece distribution both randomised) the rival predicts zero skill effect, template theory a small one. A small reliable skill effect was found.
numbers: N = 36 (BCF-rated; groups of 7 grandmasters, 12 masters/experts, then weaker players). Skill slope on fully randomised positions 0.052 (SE 0.016) per BCF point, p < .005; template-theory prediction 0.061. 100 BCF points give about 5.2% recall, about 1.25 pieces. Controls: age (about -2.6% per decade) and visual memory (not a predictor). Quadratic skill term not significant (p = .19).
limits: Effect is small; limited power to separate slopes on the other random conditions. One-tailed p values for skill. Seven participants reported guessing. Correlational design: ratings were not varied experimentally.
agent_relevance: A rival that predicts exactly zero is easy to test against a small positive effect. Use this style: pick the condition where two memory designs disagree and measure the slope, not just significance.

source: Gobet & Waters (2003) The role of constraints in expert memory
finding: Skill slope shrinks as structure is removed. Both theories got the ordering right, so only the fully random condition separated them. Slopes on the three most random conditions did not differ reliably.
numbers: Unstandardised skill slopes per BCF point (the extracted table is garbled; this row mapping is my reading): game 0.35 (R2 50%), one-third randomised 0.11 (31%), two-thirds 0.063 (26%), random 0.059 (17%), fully random 0.052 (28%).
limits: Row labels in the extracted table are misaligned, so the mapping is inferred from the text and the R2 order. Treat the middle three values as approximate.
agent_relevance: Game-like input gives about 7 times the skill slope of fully random input. Expect a pattern library's benefit to fall steeply with structural novelty, with a small non-zero floor.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis (Memory & Cognition 45)
finding: Across domains, experts recall randomised domain material better than novices. Moderate effect, high heterogeneity, signs of publication bias.
numbers: Binomial analysis: 45 studies, 55 samples, experts better in 49 of 55. Meta-analysis: 24 studies, 28 effect sizes, 903 participants; random-effects r = .41, 95% CI .29 to .51; I-squared 63.06%. Domain moderator Q(4) = 8.69, p = .069 (games .42, music .69, programming .36, sports .30, other .24). Exposure time (8 s or less vs more) Q(1) = 0.89, p = .346.
quote: experts partly base their superiority on a vaster amount of small memory structures
limits: Read through a page-summary tool, not the raw text, so opened is false. Same research group as the template theory authors. Includes studies of mixed quality.
agent_relevance: Best single estimate for the random-material effect: r about .4 before bias correction. Use it as the prior when claiming a pattern store helps on partly novel problems.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) meta-analysis of experts' memory for random material
finding: Publication bias lowers the estimate a lot. After trim-and-fill the correlation drops to .29. Dropping two problem studies leaves it about .39.
numbers: Funnel plot asymmetric; trim-and-fill imputed 8 studies, r = .29, 95% CI .17 to .41; fail-safe N = 745; sensitivity run r = .39, CI .28 to .50, I-squared 64.15%.
limits: Same caveats as b19. Trim-and-fill is an approximate correction.
agent_relevance: Quote the corrected figure (about .3) when planning. Published effects of memory-based expertise on novel stimuli are probably inflated.

source: Linhares & Brum (2007) Understanding our understanding of strategic scenarios: what role do chunks play? (Cognitive Science 31, 989-1007)
finding: Rival to the piece-on-square view. Players judged very different positions as similar when pieces played the same abstract roles. The authors say abstract roles, not exact squares, carry the key information, and put analogy at the centre.
numbers: Not obtained (no counts or effect sizes seen).
limits: Known only from a search-result abstract; the repository page returned an access-denied bot page. Not reconciled with b02, where location-specific chunks fit the numbers. The two may measure different things (recall versus similarity judgement).
agent_relevance: Competing claim to test: retrieval by abstract role versus by literal layout. Run both keys on our own problems and compare transfer.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: revisiting the chunking hypothesis (Memory 6), as reported in Gobet & Clarkson (2004)
finding: Reported replication of Chase & Simon on a computer display with a larger sample (Masters, Experts, Class A). Latency distributions were similar, but Masters' chunks were larger and fewer than in 1973.
numbers: Masters' largest chunk in recall 16.8 pieces (Chase & Simon master median: 5). Median within-glance latency 1.37 s (1998) vs 1.00 s (1973) vs 0.44 s (Gobet & Clarkson, physical board). Median between-glance latency 7.30 s on screen.
limits: Second-hand: seen through the 2004 paper, not the original. The 2004 authors note the 1998 study used only the computer task, so display and sample were confounded; their within-subject design addressed this (b14).
agent_relevance: A replication that changes the headline number (5 vs 16.8 pieces) while keeping the qualitative effect. Report both when citing chunk sizes.

source: Gobet & Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory (review sections)
finding: Lists weak points of the original chunking evidence and the rivals. Chunking fails on interference and on chunk size. Long-term working memory and constraint attunement are less explicit about chunk size and number, so they give fewer testable numbers.
numbers: 1973 theory: STM about 7 chunks; 8 s to create a chunk, 2 s to add to one. Later claims: 3 chunks (Broadbent), 4 chunks (Cowan 2001). Chi (1978) partition task: about 3 s to place pieces across cluster borders versus about 1.5 s within a cluster.
limits: Authors are chunking and template proponents. The statement that rivals cannot give numbers is theirs and may be contested by those camps.
agent_relevance: Prefer theories that give numbers we can falsify. For our schema, memory components should come with a predicted size or time that a test can break.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models (COLM 2024)
finding: A language model trained only on chess game text holds a linear board-state representation, and it can be edited by intervention. Baseline matters: a randomly initialised network also gives a decent probe score.
numbers: Board-state probe accuracy 99.6% (16-layer) and 99.1% (8-layer) vs 74.7% and 75.0% on randomised-weight models. Skill probe 90.5% and 88.6% vs 69.3% and 70.2%. Legal-move rate 99.8% (16-layer), 99.6% (8-layer). 8-layer model won 46% against Stockfish level 0 (about 1300 Elo).
limits: Trained on real games; no recall test on scrambled boards. Probes show a representation exists, not that it drives move choice (hence the interventions). Small model family.
agent_relevance: Analogue of the random-versus-game test: compare against a randomised baseline (about 75%) before crediting learned structure. Applies to any retrieval probe we build.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with large language models (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: LLM analogue of templates. A meta-buffer stores distilled high-level thought templates, retrieves one per problem and fills it in. Large gains over prompting baselines on the authors' ten tasks, biggest on tasks with a fixed solution structure (Checkmate-in-One, Game of 24).
numbers: Accuracy % (GPT-4 based): Game of 24 82.4 (ToT 74.0, plain GPT-4 3.0); Checkmate-in-One 86.4 (Meta Prompting 57.2, GoT 51.4, plain 36.4); Geometric Shapes 93.6 (78.2); Date Understanding 88.2 (79.2); Sonnet Writing 80.0 (79.6, near tie). Cost about 12% of multi-query methods.
limits: Authors' own method and benchmark set. In the text I read, templates were not shown to be tested on problems held out from the template-building problems; contamination by the test distribution is not excluded.
agent_relevance: Closest measured match to memory of solution templates that cue moves, and it includes a chess task. Cite as promising, not proof; replicate with strict held-out splits before relying on it.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts, ablations and limits
finding: Removing the meta-buffer or the problem distiller hurts most on complex tasks (Game of 24, Checkmate-in-One). With the buffer-manager, accuracy rises over four rounds of 50 new questions per benchmark; without it, no upward trend. The authors list limits.
numbers: Ablation values are in figures only (none in the text I read). Buffer-manager test: 4 rounds x 50 questions per benchmark. Stated limits: smaller gains on tasks needing human-like creativity; templates distilled by a weaker model are worse.
quote: our method's enhancements are limited when addressing problems requiring human-like creativity
limits: No error bars or repeated seeds in the text. Rising accuracy over rounds could also reflect easier later samples or leakage between rounds.
agent_relevance: Gains from stored templates depend on task structure and on the quality of the model that wrote the templates. Seed templates only from a strong model, and expect little on open-ended tasks.

source: Ciancarini & Pareschi (2026) What counts as strategic reasoning? A systematic mapping of chess research on humans, engines, and language models (arXiv 2609.18286)
finding: Mapping of 84 study families. LLM chess work centres on state representation and generalisation. Evaluations now use novel positions, Chess960 and controlled perturbations to separate memorised patterns from transferable skill, the same logic as the random-position control.
numbers: 84 core study families. Cites Schut et al. (2025): four elite grandmasters improved after seeing machine-derived concept prototypes.
limits: Secondary survey; I read selected sections only. Counts are the survey's own, not re-checked. Study quality not weighed.
agent_relevance: Perturbation tests (Chess960 style) are the accepted check for pattern-memory claims in LLMs. Use matched perturbed variants for any template-memory evaluation.

source: Schut et al. (2023/2025) Bridging the human-AI knowledge gap: concept discovery and transfer in AlphaZero (PNAS 122)
finding: Concept prototypes extracted from AlphaZero were shown to four top grandmasters, who improved on the presented concept positions afterwards. A measured case of pattern teaching with transfer to humans.
numbers: Four grandmasters. Accuracy gain and puzzle count not available on the abstract page.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Tiny sample. Gains reported on the concept-prototype positions themselves; wider transfer not seen here.
agent_relevance: A selected, teachable pattern set can move expert performance. Filtering candidate patterns for novelty and teachability is a design idea to test, with small-N caution.

source: Cooke et al. (1993) nine-board recall, as reported in Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory
finding: An independent lab's nine-board study agreed in outline with Gobet & Simon: percentages fell with more boards while the count of pieces recalled rose.
numbers: Two Masters, 8 s per board, up to nine boards: about 90% (one board), about 50% (five), about 40% (nine). De Groot guessing baseline 43.7%.
limits: Figures estimated from a graph by Gobet and Simon, not read from the original paper. Two subjects.
agent_relevance: Two labs converge on the same limit, a good sign for the effect. It also shows a ceiling: an agent holding many cases at once should expect a similar fall-off.

source: Saariluoma (1984, 1994) quadrant and hybrid position experiments, as described in Gobet & Simon (1996)
finding: Boundary condition: if the pieces stay in their real locations, hybrid positions built from four different games are recalled about as well as real game positions. Swapping quadrants to wrong places drops recall to or below random level for the swapped parts.
numbers: Hybrid (location kept): about game-position level. Swapped quadrants: below random-position level for the swapped parts. Class C to Expert players; exact numbers not given in the Gobet & Simon paper.
limits: Second-hand account; Saariluoma's own papers were not opened. Some hybrid positions were illegal.
agent_relevance: Local, in-place patterns carry the effect; the global gist is not needed. For retrieval, local matches may suffice, and a whole-problem type label may not be required.
